words.meaning: austerity, recitation and devotion to the Lord

translations.text: Austerity, recitation and devotion to the Lord are the yoga of action.

notes: Vyāsa: the first pāda taught yoga for one whose mind is absorbed; this begins how one whose mind is turned outwards may also come to yoga. Yoga does not succeed for one without austerity: the impurity, coloured by beginningless action and affliction, is not broken up without it; but it is to be practised so as not to disturb the clearness of the mind. Recitation is the repetition of Om and other purifying formulas, or the study of the scriptures of liberation. Devotion to the Lord is offering all actions to the supreme teacher, or renouncing their fruit.

translations.text: It is for bringing about meditative absorption and for thinning the afflictions.

notes: Vyāsa: the afflictions, once thinned, will be made barren like burnt seeds by the fire of reflection. Then the subtle wisdom, the discernment that sattva and the Puruṣa are different, untouched by the afflictions and its task finished, will be fit to return to its source.

words.meaning: ignorance, the sense of ‘I am’, attachment, aversion and clinging to life

translations.text: The afflictions are ignorance, the sense of ‘I am’, attachment, aversion and clinging to life.

notes: Vyāsa: the afflictions are the five errors. When active they strengthen the working of the guṇas, keep change going, swell the stream of cause and effect, and, helping one another, bring about the ripening of action.

words.meaning: whether dormant, thinned, interrupted or active

translations.text: Ignorance is the field of the others, whether they are dormant, thinned, interrupted or active.

notes: Vyāsa: ignorance is the field, the breeding ground, of the other four. Dormant: resting in the mind as a mere power, in the state of a seed; it wakes when its object comes before it. For one who has reflection the seed of the afflictions is burnt, and it does not wake even when the object is before him: he is called one whose afflictions are destroyed, skilled, in his last body. This burnt-seed state is a fifth state of the afflictions and is found in him alone. Thinned: weakened by cultivating the opposite. Interrupted: appearing again and again with breaks, as anger is not seen while attachment is at work; and Caitra, attached to one woman, is not thereby averse to the others: there his attachment is at work, elsewhere it is yet to come. Active: at work on its object.

Vyāsa: none of the four ceases to be an affliction; the names mark only the state each is in: turned back by cultivating the opposite, or brought out by what manifests it. All of them are kinds of ignorance, for ignorance runs through them all: they follow whatever ignorance gives shape to, they are found while the mistaken notion lasts, and they waste away as ignorance wastes away.

words.meaning: in what is impermanent, impure, painful and not the self
the seeing of the permanent, the pure, the pleasant and the self

translations.text: Ignorance is seeing the permanent, the pure, the pleasant and the self in what is impermanent, impure, painful and not the self.

notes: Vyāsa: the permanent in the impermanent: ‘the earth is lasting, the gods are deathless’. The pure in the impure: the body, which the wise know to be impure from its place of origin, its seed, its sustenance, its discharges and its end; yet a girl is thought lovely as the new moon. The pleasant in the painful (2.15). The self in what is not the self: outer things, the body, or the mind. This fourfold ignorance is the root of the stream of afflictions and of the store of action. It is not the mere absence of knowledge but another knowledge, contrary to knowledge, as amitra is not ‘no friend’ but an enemy.

words.meaning: of the power of the seer and the power of seeing

translations.text: The sense of ‘I am’ is the power of the seer and the power of seeing becoming, as it were, one self.

notes: Vyāsa: the Puruṣa is the power that sees, the understanding the power by which seeing is done; their seeming to take one form is the affliction. Experience arises when the powers of the experiencer and the experienced, wholly distinct and unmixed, come as if to be undivided; when each is known in its own nature there is only soleness, and no experience.

translations.text: Attachment is that which follows on pleasure.

notes: Vyāsa: the greed, thirst and craving for pleasure or its means, in one who has known pleasure and remembers it.

translations.text: Aversion is that which follows on pain.

notes: Vyāsa: the resistance, anger and wish to strike at pain or its means, in one who has known pain and remembers it.

padaccheda.deva: स्व-रस-वाही विदुषः अपि तथा रूढः अभिनिवेशः

words.meaning: flowing on by its own force

grammar.en: past passive participle m. nom. sg.

translations.text: Clinging to life flows on by its own force, and is rooted likewise even in the learned.

notes: Vyāsa: every living being has this constant wish for itself: ‘may I not cease to be; may I be’. It could not arise in one who had not known death, so it shows the experience of earlier births. This fear of death is seen even in a worm just born, where perception, inference and scripture cannot account for it. As it is found in the wholly dull, so it is rooted in the learned who know the beginning and the end, for the latent trace of the pain of death is the same in both.

words.meaning: to be given up by the return to the source

translations.text: When subtle, they are to be given up by the return (of the mind) to its source.

notes: Vyāsa: the five afflictions, become like burnt seeds, pass away together with the yogin's mind when, its task done, it dissolves.

words.meaning: to be given up by meditation

translations.text: Their activities are to be given up by meditation.

notes: Vyāsa: the gross activities of the afflictions, thinned by the yoga of action, are to be given up by the meditation of reflection until they are made subtle, like burnt seeds. As the gross dirt of a cloth is shaken off first and the fine dirt removed afterwards with effort, so the gross activities have a slight opponent and the subtle a great one.

words.meaning: to be experienced in the present birth or in one unseen

translations.text: The store of action, rooted in the afflictions, is to be experienced in the present birth or in one unseen.

notes: Vyāsa: the store of merit and demerit is born of desire, greed, delusion and anger. Merit gained with keen ardour by mantra, austerity and absorption, or by worship of the Lord, the gods and great seers, ripens at once; so does the evil of repeated harm done, under strong affliction, to the frightened, the sick and the wretched, or to those who trust one. Thus the boy Nandīśvara left the human state and became a god, and Nahuṣa, lord of the gods, became an animal.

words.meaning: birth, span of life and experience

translations.text: While the root is there, its ripening is birth, span of life and experience.

notes: Vyāsa: the store of action begins to ripen while the afflictions are there, not when that root is cut: rice grains sprout while they are in the husk and unburnt, not when husked or burnt. The ripening is of three kinds, birth, span of life and experience.

Vyāsa asks whether one action causes one birth or many, and whether many actions cause many births or one. Not one action one birth: with the countless actions heaped up from time without beginning and those of the present, there would be no rule for the order of their fruits, and people would lose all confidence. Not one action many births: there would be no time left for the rest to ripen. Not many actions many births: the births cannot be together, and if they come in turn the first fault returns. So the varied store of merit and demerit made between birth and death, with some actions chief and others subordinate, is brought out by death, rolls into one, brings death about and makes one birth; that birth has its span of life from the same action, and in that span its experience. The store is therefore said to belong to one life and to have three ripenings.

Vyāsa: action to be experienced in the present birth begins one ripening, experience, or two, span of life and experience, as with Nandīśvara and Nahuṣa. The latent tendencies are another matter: made by the experience of afflictions, action and ripening, they have filled the mind from time without beginning, as a fishing net is covered all over with knots; they come from many lives. They are the latent impressions that cause memory.

Vyāsa: the rule of one life holds for the store whose ripening is fixed and which is to be experienced in the next birth. Action to be experienced in an unseen birth, whose ripening is not fixed, has three courses. It may perish unripened, as dark action perishes here itself when bright action arises. It may be merged in a chief action: a slight admixture of evil does not suffice to take away the good, and makes only a small deduction even in heaven. Or it may stay for a long time, overpowered by a chief action whose ripening is fixed, until a like action that manifests it turns it towards ripening. Because the place, time and occasion of that ripening cannot be determined, the course of action is varied and hard to know. An exception does not set aside the general rule: the store of action belongs to one life.

words.meaning: have joy and distress as their fruit
because they are caused by merit and demerit

translations.text: They have joy and distress as their fruit, because they are caused by merit and demerit.

notes: Vyāsa: birth, span of life and experience bear pleasure when caused by merit and pain when caused by demerit. And as this pain is disagreeable, so for the yogin there is pain, disagreeable, even at the time of pleasure from objects.

words.meaning: because of the pains of change, of distress and of latent impressions
because the workings of the guṇas conflict

translations.text: Because of the pains of change, of distress and of latent impressions, and because the workings of the guṇas conflict, all is only pain for the discerning.

notes: Vyāsa: the pain of change: pleasure is shot through with attachment, so it leaves a store of action; and the senses cannot be freed of thirst by enjoyment, which only makes craving and the senses' skill grow. He who seeks pleasure is like one who, fearing a scorpion's sting, is bitten by a snake. The pain of distress: distress is shot through with aversion; seeking the means of pleasure one acts with body, speech and mind, helps some and harms others, and heaps up dharma and adharma. The pain of impressions: from pleasure and pain come their latent impressions, and from experience a new store of action. This beginningless stream of pain troubles only the yogin, who is as sensitive as the eyeball, which a thread of wool hurts though it does not hurt other limbs.

Vyāsa: pleasure in objects has been called ignorance. The stilling of the senses when they are satisfied is pleasure; their restlessness from greed is pain. The other man takes up again and again the pain his own action brings and drops it again and again; shot through on every side with ignorance by a mind varied with latent tendencies that have no beginning, following ‘I’ and ‘mine’ where they should be given up, he is flooded birth after birth by the three kinds of distress, from outer causes, inner causes and both. Seeing himself and all living beings carried along by this stream of pain, the yogin takes refuge in right seeing, the cause of the ending of all pain.

Vyāsa: the guṇas of the understanding, illumination, activity and inertia, help one another to produce a calm, a violent or a dull cognition; their working is unsteady. As medical science has four parts, disease, its cause, health and the remedy, so has this teaching: the cycle of birth and death, its cause, liberation, and the means to liberation. The cycle, full of pain, is what is to be avoided; the conjunction of Prakṛti and the Puruṣa is its cause; the final ceasing of that conjunction is the avoidance; and right seeing is the means.

Vyāsa: the guṇas in their excess of form and of working conflict with one another, while in their ordinary measure they work together; each, leaning on the others, gives rise to cognitions of pleasure, pain and delusion, so that all have all forms, the difference lying in which is chief. Hence all is pain for the discerning. The seed from which this great mass of pain grows is ignorance, and right seeing is the cause of its ceasing. The own nature of the one who avoids can be neither something to be taken up nor something to be avoided: if it were avoided, the doctrine of annihilation would follow; if taken up, the doctrine that it has a cause; with both set aside, the doctrine of the eternal. That is right seeing.

translations.text: The pain that has not yet come is what is to be avoided.

notes: Vyāsa: past pain has been lived through and present pain is being experienced in its own moment; only pain that is yet to come can be avoided.

words.meaning: of the seer and the seen
the cause of what is to be avoided

translations.text: The conjunction of the seer and the seen is the cause of what is to be avoided.

notes: Vyāsa: the seer is the Puruṣa, who is aware of the understanding; the seen is all the properties that rest on the sattva of the understanding. The seen, like a magnet, serves merely by being near, and belongs to the Puruṣa as its owner. Their beginningless conjunction, made for a purpose, is the cause of pain. As one who knows the sole of the foot that can be pierced, the thorn that pierces, and the remedy of not stepping on it or wearing a shoe, escapes that pain, so here: rajas is what burns and sattva what is burnt, not the changeless knower of the field; but when sattva is burnt, the Puruṣa, following its form, seems to burn too.

words.meaning: whose nature is illumination, activity and inertia
consisting of the elements and the senses

translations.text: The seen has illumination, activity and inertia as its nature, consists of the elements and the senses, and exists for experience and liberation.

notes: Vyāsa: sattva has illumination as its nature, rajas activity, tamas inertia. These guṇas colour one another, change, join and part, and take shape by leaning on one another, yet their powers stay unmixed; they serve by mere nearness, like a magnet, for the Puruṣa's purpose. They are what the word pradhāna means, and are called the seen. It changes into the elements, earth and the rest, subtle and gross, and into the senses, hearing and the rest, subtle and gross.

Vyāsa: experience is the ascertaining of the guṇas as wished or unwished, without division (from the Puruṣa); liberation is the ascertaining of the experiencer's own nature. Both are made by the understanding and are in it alone; they are ascribed to the Puruṣa as victory or defeat, which is the soldiers', is ascribed to their lord, for he enjoys its fruit. Bondage is the understanding's not having finished the Puruṣa's purpose; release is the finishing of it.

Vyāsa: apart from these two there is no other seeing. In the same way grasping, retaining, reasoning for and against, knowledge of the truth and resolve are in the understanding, and their existence is superimposed on the Puruṣa, for he enjoys their fruit.

words.meaning: the particular, the unparticular, the mere mark and the unmarked

translations.text: The stages of the guṇas are the particular, the unparticular, the mere mark and the unmarked.

notes: Vyāsa: the particulars are sixteen: the five elements, space, air, fire, water and earth; the five senses of knowledge; the five organs of action; and the mind, the eleventh, which serves all. The unparticulars are six: the five subtle elements of sound, touch, colour, taste and smell, and the bare sense of ‘I am’. These six are changes of the great one (mahat), which is bare existence, the mere mark. Beyond it is the unmarked, pradhāna, the unmanifest, neither existent nor non-existent, into which they return.

Vyāsa: the Puruṣa's purpose is not the cause of the unmarked state, so it is called eternal; of the other three states it is the cause, so they are called non-eternal. The guṇas themselves neither perish nor arise; they only seem to, through their manifestations, as Devadatta is said to grow poor because his cows die, not because he himself is lessened. The particulars change into no further principle.

Vyāsa: sound and the other subtle elements have one, two, three, four and five characteristics in turn. The mere mark lies next to the unmarked; mixed in it, it is distinguished out of it, since the order of change is not overstepped; so the six unparticulars are distinguished out of the mere mark, and the elements and senses out of the unparticulars. The changes that the particulars do have, of property, temporal character and condition, are explained later (3.13).

words.meaning: looking on by way of the cognition

translations.text: The seer is seeing alone; though pure, he looks on by way of the cognition.

notes: Vyāsa: ‘seeing alone’: the power of seeing itself, untouched by any qualification. This Puruṣa is aware of the understanding. He is not like it, and not wholly unlike it. Not like it: the understanding changes, since its object is now known and now unknown, while the Puruṣa's object is always known, which shows that he does not change; the understanding works by combining and so serves another, while the Puruṣa is for himself; it is of the three guṇas and so not conscious, while he is the onlooker of the guṇas. Not wholly unlike it: though pure, he looks on the cognition that belongs to the understanding, and so appears as if of its nature though he is not.

translations.text: The being of the seen is only for his sake.

notes: Vyāsa: the seen has become the object of the Puruṣa, whose form is seeing, so its being, that is, its own nature, is for his sake alone. When experience and liberation are accomplished it is no longer seen by the Puruṣa; having lost its nature it should perish, yet it does not (2.22).

lines.iast: kṛtārthaṃ prati naṣṭam apy anaṣṭaṃ tadanyasādhāraṇatvāt

padaccheda.deva: कृत-अर्थम् प्रति नष्टम् अपि अनष्टम् तत्-अन्य-साधारणत्वात्

grammar.en: past passive participle n. nom. sg.

words.meaning: because it is common to others than him

translations.text: Though it has ceased for one whose purpose is accomplished, it has not ceased, because it is common to others than him.

notes: Vyāsa: the seen has ceased for the one skilled Puruṣa, but not for the unskilled, for whom its purpose is not accomplished. So, the powers of seer and seen being eternal, their conjunction is said to be without beginning.

words.meaning: of the two powers, the owned and the owner
the cause of the apprehension of their own nature

translations.text: The conjunction is the cause of the apprehension of the own nature of the two powers, the owned and the owner.

notes: Vyāsa: the Puruṣa, the owner, is joined with the seen, his own, in order to see. The apprehension of the seen from that conjunction is experience; the apprehension of the seer's own nature is liberation. The conjunction lasts until seeing is done, so seeing is called the cause of disjunction, and non-seeing, its opposite, the cause of conjunction. Seeing is not here itself the cause of release: when non-seeing is absent, bondage is absent, and that is release.

Vyāsa: when seeing is there, non-seeing, the cause of bondage, is destroyed; in that sense seeing, that is knowledge, is called the cause of soleness. What then is this non-seeing? He sets out eight alternatives found in the teaching. (1) The guṇas' having a task still to do. (2) The non-arising of the chief mind, which shows objects to its owner, whose nature is seeing: the absence of seeing while his own seen is there. (3) The guṇas' having a purpose. (4) Ignorance, held back together with its own mind, as the seed of that mind's arising. (5) The coming out of the impression of motion when the impression of rest is spent: for pradhāna, if it only rested, would make no modification, and if it only moved, modification would be eternal; in neither case would it be pradhāna. (6) The power of seeing itself, since pradhāna acts in order to make itself known. (7) A property of both, the seen and the Puruṣa. (8) Seeing, knowledge itself, is the non-seeing, as some say.

Vyāsa: this multitude of alternatives concerns the conjunction of the guṇas with all Puruṣas in common. The conjunction of the inward consciousness with its own understanding is taken up in the next sūtra.

translations.text: The cause of that is ignorance.

notes: Vyāsa: ‘of that’: of the conjunction of the inner consciousness with its own understanding. Ignorance here is the latent tendency of false knowledge. An understanding steeped in it does not reach the end of its task, the seeing of the Puruṣa, and comes back with its task still to do; when it ends in the seeing of the Puruṣa, its task done and non-seeing gone, there is no cause of bondage and it does not come back.

padaccheda.iast: tat-abhāvāt saṃyoga-abhāvaḥ hānam tat dṛśeḥ kaivalyam
padaccheda.deva: तत्-अभावात् संयोग-अभावः हानम् तत् दृशेः कैवल्यम्

translations.text: From the absence of that, the absence of conjunction is the avoidance; that is the soleness of the seer.

notes: Vyāsa: when non-seeing is absent, the conjunction of the understanding and the Puruṣa is absent: the final ceasing of bondage. This is the avoidance. The soleness of the seer is the Puruṣa's being unmixed, never again joined with the guṇas. Then the Puruṣa rests in his own nature.

translations.text: The unwavering vision of discernment is the means of avoidance.

notes: Vyāsa: the vision of discernment is the cognition that sattva and the Puruṣa are different. While false knowledge has not ceased it wavers. When false knowledge has become like a burnt seed, unable to sprout, the stream of discerning cognition runs clear in a sattva washed of the dust of the afflictions. This is the path to release.

translations.text: His wisdom, at its final stage, is sevenfold.

notes: Vyāsa: ‘his’: of the one in whom this vision has arisen. Four are the freedom of wisdom from its task: what is to be avoided is fully known, and nothing remains to be known; the causes of what is to be avoided have wasted away, and nothing remains to be wasted; the avoidance has been made present by the absorption of cessation; the means of avoidance, the vision of discernment, has been cultivated. Three are the freedom of the mind: the understanding has done its task; the guṇas, like stones fallen from a mountain peak, with nowhere to rest, go towards dissolution in their cause and set with it, not to arise again; and in that state the Puruṣa, beyond all tie with the guṇas, is the light of his own nature alone, stainless and sole.

words.meaning: from the practice of the limbs of yoga

translations.text: From the practice of the limbs of yoga, as impurity wastes away, the light of knowledge grows, up to the vision of discernment.

notes: Vyāsa: the impurity is the fivefold error. As the means are practised it thins, and as it wastes the light of knowledge grows by the same steps, up to the vision of discernment, that is, the knowing of the nature of the guṇas and the Puruṣa. The practice of the limbs is the cause of separation from impurity, as an axe is of what is cut, and the cause of attaining discernment, as dharma is of happiness. He then lists the nine kinds of cause known to the teaching: of arising, staying, manifestation, change, cognition, attainment, separation, difference and support.

words.meaning: the restraints, the observances, posture, control of the breath, withdrawal of the senses, fixing of the mind, meditation and meditative absorption

translations.text: The eight limbs are the restraints, the observances, posture, control of the breath, withdrawal of the senses, fixing of the mind, meditation and meditative absorption.

words.meaning: non-harming, truthfulness, non-stealing, continence and non-possession

translations.text: The restraints are non-harming, truthfulness, non-stealing, continence and non-possession.

notes: Vyāsa: non-harming is doing no injury to any being, in any way, at any time. The other restraints and observances are rooted in it and are taken up only to make it spotless. Truthfulness is speech and mind that agree with the fact, as seen, inferred or heard; speech is uttered to pass one's knowledge to another, and must not deceive, mislead or be empty. It is meant for the good of all beings: if what is said harms beings it is not truth but evil, so let one speak the truth after weighing the good of all beings. Stealing is taking others' goods against the teaching; non-stealing is its refusal, in the form of not coveting. Continence is the control of the hidden organ of generation. Non-possession is not taking objects to oneself, seeing the faults of getting, guarding, losing, clinging to and harming for them.

words.meaning: not limited by kind, place, time or occasion

translations.text: Not limited by kind, place, time or occasion, and holding at every level, they are the great vow.

notes: Vyāsa: non-harming limited by kind: the fisherman harms fish only. By place: ‘I will not kill at a holy place’. By time: ‘not on the fourteenth day, not on a holy day’. By occasion: ‘I will kill only for the gods and brahmins’, or as warriors do harm only in battle. Kept without these limits, in every state and towards every object, with no exception, they are the great vow.

words.meaning: purity, contentment, austerity, recitation and devotion to the Lord

translations.text: The observances are purity, contentment, austerity, recitation and devotion to the Lord.

notes: Vyāsa: outer purity is that got by earth, water and the like, and by eating pure food; inner purity is the washing away of the stains of the mind. Contentment is not wishing for more than the means at hand. Austerity is bearing the pairs: hunger and thirst, cold and heat, standing and sitting, and the two kinds of silence; and the vows such as the kṛcchra and cāndrāyaṇa. Recitation is the study of the scriptures of liberation, or the repetition of Om. Devotion to the Lord is offering all actions to that supreme teacher.

translations.text: When contrary thoughts oppress, the opposite is to be cultivated.

notes: Vyāsa: when thoughts of harming and the like arise, ‘I will kill him who wronged me, I will lie, I will take his goods’, let him reflect: ‘Burning on the fierce coals of the cycle of birth and death, I took refuge in the dharma of yoga by giving safety to all beings. If I take up again what I gave up, I am like a dog that licks its own vomit.’

lines.deva: वितर्का हिंसादयः कृतकारितानुमोदिता लोभक्रोधमोहपूर्वका मृदुमध्याधिमात्रा दुःखाज्ञानानन्तफला इति प्रतिपक्षभावनम्

padaccheda.iast: vitarkāḥ hiṃsā-ādayaḥ kṛta-kārita-anumoditāḥ lobha-krodha-moha-pūrvakāḥ mṛdu-madhya-adhimātrāḥ duḥkha-ajñāna-ananta-phalāḥ iti pratipakṣa-bhāvanam
padaccheda.deva: वितर्काः हिंसा-आदयः कृत-कारित-अनुमोदिताः लोभ-क्रोध-मोह-पूर्वकाः मृदु-मध्य-अधिमात्राः दुःख-अज्ञान-अनन्त-फलाः इति प्रतिपक्ष-भावनम्

words.meaning: done, caused to be done or approved
preceded by greed, anger or delusion
having pain and ignorance as their endless fruit

translations.text: Contrary thoughts, harming and the rest, whether done, caused to be done or approved, preceded by greed, anger or delusion, mild, moderate or intense, have pain and ignorance as their endless fruit: such is the cultivation of the opposite.

notes: Vyāsa: harming is of three kinds, done, caused and approved; each from greed (for meat or hide), from anger (‘he wronged me’) or from delusion (‘it will be my dharma’); each of these mild, moderate or intense: twenty-seven kinds; and each of those again threefold: eighty-one. So too with falsehood and the rest. He who harms first takes away his victim's strength, then gives him pain with a weapon, then takes his life; for this his own means of living lose their strength, he suffers pain in hell and as an animal or a ghost, and lives wishing for death at every moment. Reflecting thus on the unwished ripening that follows such thoughts, let him not set his mind on them.

translations.text: When non-harming is firmly established, enmity is given up in his presence.

notes: Vyāsa: by all living beings.

words.meaning: the being the ground of action and its fruit

translations.text: When truthfulness is firmly established, action and its fruit rest on him.

notes: Vyāsa: if he says ‘be a man of dharma’, the man becomes one; if he says ‘attain heaven’, he attains heaven. His speech is unfailing.

translations.text: When non-stealing is firmly established, all jewels come to him.

notes: Vyāsa: jewels from every quarter come to him.

translations.text: When continence is firmly established, vigour is gained.

notes: Vyāsa: by gaining it he heightens his powers unhindered; and, perfected, he is able to plant knowledge in his pupils.

words.meaning: full knowledge of the how of his births

translations.text: When non-possession is steady, there is full knowledge of the how of his births.

notes: Vyāsa: ‘Who was I? How was I? What is this, and how? What shall we be, and how?’ The wish to know his own state in the past, the future and the present is fulfilled of itself. These are the perfections that come when the restraints are steady.

translations.text: From purity come distaste for one's own body and non-contact with others.

notes: Vyāsa: he who practises purity sees the faults of the body and does not cling to it. Seeing the body's nature, wishing to leave even his own, and finding it not clean though he washes it with earth and water, how should he join with the wholly unclean bodies of others?

words.meaning: purity of sattva, gladness, one-pointedness, mastery of the senses and fitness to see the self

translations.text: And (there come) purity of sattva, gladness, one-pointedness, mastery of the senses and fitness to see the self.

notes: Vyāsa: ‘there come’ completes the sentence. In the pure there is purity of sattva; from it gladness, from that one-pointedness, from that mastery of the senses, and from that the fitness of the sattva of the understanding to see the self.

translations.text: From contentment, unsurpassed happiness is gained.

notes: Vyāsa: as it is said: ‘The pleasure of desire in this world and the great pleasure of heaven are not worth a sixteenth part of the happiness of the wasting away of thirst.’

words.meaning: the perfection of the body and the senses
through the wasting away of impurity

translations.text: From austerity, through the wasting away of impurity, comes the perfection of the body and the senses.

notes: Vyāsa: austerity, as it is carried out, destroys the stain of impurity that covers. When that is gone there is perfection of the body, minuteness and the rest, and of the senses, hearing and seeing from afar and the like.

translations.text: From recitation comes communion with the chosen deity.

notes: Vyāsa: gods, seers and perfected ones come into the sight of one given to recitation, and serve his work.

translations.text: From devotion to the Lord comes the perfection of absorption.

notes: Vyāsa: for one who has offered his whole being to the Lord there is perfection of absorption, by which he knows all that he wishes to know, truly, in another place, another body and another time. Then his wisdom knows the thing as it is.

translations.text: Posture is steady and easy.

notes: Vyāsa: such as the lotus posture, the auspicious posture, the svastika, the staff posture, the one with a support, the couch, the seats of the curlew, the elephant and the camel, the even pose, the steady and easy, and the one as is comfortable.

words.meaning: by the slackening of effort and by coalescence with the infinite

translations.text: (It comes) by the slackening of effort and by coalescence with the infinite.

notes: Vyāsa: ‘it comes’ completes the sentence. Posture is perfected when effort ceases, so that the limbs do not tremble; or the mind, coalesced with the infinite, brings posture about.

words.meaning: the not being struck by the pairs of opposites

translations.text: From that, one is not struck by the pairs of opposites.

notes: Vyāsa: having mastered posture, he is not overcome by pairs such as cold and heat.

words.meaning: of the in-breath and the out-breath
the cutting off of the movement

translations.text: That being so, control of the breath is the cutting off of the movement of the in-breath and the out-breath.

notes: Vyāsa: when posture is mastered. The in-breath is the drinking in of the outer air; the out-breath is the sending out of the air within. The cutting off of their movement is the absence of both.

words.meaning: whose working is outer, inner or arrested

grammar.en: past passive participle m. nom. sg.

translations.text: Its working is outer, inner or arrested; measured by place, time and number, it becomes long and subtle.

notes: Vyāsa: outer: where the absence of movement follows the out-breath. Inner: where it follows the in-breath. The third, arrested: where both are absent by a single effort, as water dropped on a heated stone shrinks from every side. All three are measured by place (‘so far is its range’), by time (the number of moments), and by number (so many in-breaths and out-breaths to the first stroke, so many to the second, to the third; so mild, moderate, intense). Practised thus it becomes long and subtle.

words.meaning: passing beyond the outer and the inner range

translations.text: The fourth passes beyond the outer and the inner range.

notes: Vyāsa: the outer range, measured by place, time and number, is passed beyond; so too the inner. The absence of movement of both that follows this, coming by degrees as each stage is won, is the fourth. The third is an absence of movement begun at once, without regard to range; the fourth comes after the ranges of in-breath and out-breath are ascertained and passed beyond: that is the difference.

translations.text: From that, the covering of the light is worn away.

notes: Vyāsa: for the yogin who practises control of the breath, the action that covers discerning knowledge wastes away. That action, which veils the light and binds to the cycle of birth and death, grows weak and wastes at every moment. As it is said: ‘There is no austerity higher than control of the breath; from it come the cleansing of stains and the light of knowledge.’

words.meaning: for the fixings of the mind

translations.text: And the mind becomes fit for the fixings of the mind.

notes: Vyāsa: from the practice of control of the breath alone, by the saying ‘or by the breathing out and the holding of the breath’ (1.34).

words.meaning: when not joined to their own objects
the following of the mind's own nature

translations.text: Withdrawal is the senses' following, as it were, the mind's own nature when they are not joined to their own objects.

notes: Vyāsa: when the mind has ceased, the senses have ceased like it; they need no other means, as the mastery of each sense otherwise would. As bees fly up after the king bee when he flies up and settle when he settles, so the senses cease when the mind ceases.

translations.text: From that comes the highest mastery of the senses.

notes: Vyāsa: some say mastery of the senses is not being addicted to sound and the other objects; others, contact with them that is not forbidden, or at one's own will; others, knowing them without pleasure or pain, attachment and aversion being absent. Jaigīṣavya says it is their not being perceived at all, the mind being one-pointed. This last is the highest mastery: when the mind has ceased the senses have ceased, and the yogin needs no further effort.
